blocks.text: A 26-year-old woman wakes with a drooping left side of her face. She cannot close her left eye, cannot raise her left eyebrow, and her smile is lopsided; food collects in her left cheek. Everything below the face works. One nerve, in one narrow bony canal, has stopped transmitting.

blocks.markdown: The twelve pairs of **cranial nerves** are numbered in the order of attachment, rostral to caudal. Each carries some combination of **special sensory**, **general sensory**, **somatic motor** and **parasympathetic** fibres. A systematic grasp of what each nerve does is the basis for bedside localisation: the examiner asks what function is lost and traces the nerve's course for a lesion site.

rows: Vision; afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex
Superior, inferior and medial rectus and inferior oblique; levator palpebrae superioris (eyelid); parasympathetic to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle
Sensation from face, scalp, cornea, mouth; motor to muscles of mastication
Muscles of facial expression; taste from anterior two thirds of tongue; lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands; stapedius
Taste and sensation from posterior third of tongue and pharynx (afferent of gag reflex); stylopharyngeus; parotid gland; carotid sinus afferents
Motor to pharynx, soft palate and larynx; parasympathetic to thoracic and abdominal viscera; sensation from pharynx, larynx and viscera
Intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles (except palatoglossus)
blocks.caption: Eye movements by shorthand: LR6 SO4 AO3, meaning lateral rectus is CN VI, superior oblique CN IV, all others CN III.

blocks.markdown:
**Bedside testing: the oculomotor nerve (III).** Inspect the eyelids for **ptosis** (levator palpebrae). Examine the **pupils**: size, shape, and response to light (direct and consensual) and to accommodation. Test **eye movements** by asking the patient to follow a finger through an 'H' pattern while the head is held still, asking about double vision (diplopia). A complete CN III palsy leaves the eye pointing **down and out** (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique), with **ptosis** and a **dilated, unreactive pupil** because the parasympathetic fibres are lost.

**The facial nerve (VII).** Ask the patient to raise the eyebrows, screw the eyes tightly shut, show the teeth, smile and puff out the cheeks. Check taste and the corneal reflex if needed. The facial motor nucleus has two parts: the part serving the **upper face** receives **bilateral** cortical input, while the part serving the **lower face** receives **contralateral** cortical input only. So an **upper motor neurone (UMN)** lesion above the nucleus (a hemisphere stroke) weakens the lower face on the opposite side but **spares the forehead**, whereas a **lower motor neurone (LMN)** lesion of the nerve or nucleus (Bell palsy) weakens the **entire** ipsilateral face including the forehead.

blocks.title: UMN versus LMN facial weakness
blocks.prompt: Patient A cannot wrinkle the right forehead or close the right eye, and the right mouth droops. Patient B has right mouth droop but can wrinkle both sides of the forehead. Localise each.

steps.text: Patient A has weakness of the whole right face, including the upper face. This is an LMN pattern: a lesion of the right facial nerve or nucleus.
Patient B has weakness of the lower face only, because the upper face has bilateral cortical innervation and is spared.
Right lower-face weakness with forehead sparing is an UMN lesion in the left hemisphere (corticobulbar fibres cross to the contralateral lower-face nucleus).

blocks.answer: A: right LMN facial nerve (peripheral) lesion; B: left UMN (central) lesion such as a left hemisphere stroke.

blocks.markdown: **The vagus nerve (X).** Listen to the voice (hoarseness suggests recurrent laryngeal involvement) and ask about swallowing. Ask the patient to say 'ahh' and watch the **soft palate**: normally the palate rises symmetrically and the uvula stays central. With a unilateral vagal lesion the weak side fails to lift, so the **uvula deviates away from the side of the lesion**. The **gag reflex** tests the glossopharyngeal nerve (afferent) and the vagus (efferent). Cough is also assessed.

blocks.title: Uvula deviation
blocks.prompt: On saying 'ahh' the patient's uvula deviates to the left. Which side is the lesion, and why?

steps.text: The palatal muscles (levator veli palatini) elevate the palate through vagal motor fibres. The normal side pulls the uvula toward itself.
The healthy side contracts and pulls the uvula to its own side, away from the paralysed side.
The uvula points left, so the left side is the strong (normal) side and the right vagus is weak.

blocks.answer: A right vagal lesion: the uvula deviates away from the weak side.

blocks.markdown:
**Localising an isolated palsy along its course.** Knowing the route of each nerve lets the examiner predict the site.

- **Oculomotor (III)** passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and alongside the posterior communicating artery. Compression (for example an aneurysm) affects the **superficial parasympathetic fibres first**, producing a dilated pupil. In contrast, **microvascular ischaemia** (as in diabetes) tends to affect the nerve's core and **spares the pupil**.
- **Abducens (VI)** has a **long intracranial course** and can be stretched by raised intracranial pressure: a unilateral or bilateral VI palsy is a classic **false-localising sign**.
- **Facial (VII)** in the facial canal: Bell palsy. At the **cerebellopontine angle**, the VII and VIII nerves lie together (and V nearby), so a tumour there produces facial weakness with deafness and tinnitus.
- **Hypoglossal (XII)** palsy: the tongue deviates **toward** the side of an LMN lesion.

blocks.title: Pupil involvement in a third nerve palsy
blocks.text: A third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil should raise suspicion of compression and needs urgent imaging. A pupil-sparing third nerve palsy is more often ischaemic (microvascular). The pupil is spared because parasympathetic fibres run on the outside of the nerve and have a separate blood supply.

items: Tongue deviation points to the weak side in an LMN lesion of XII.
Uvular deviation points away from the weak side in a vagal lesion.
UMN facial palsy spares the forehead; LMN facial palsy does not.
An isolated CN VI palsy can be a false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure.

points: Each cranial nerve has defined sensory, motor and parasympathetic functions; eye movements follow the rule LR6 SO4 AO3.
Bedside tests: oculomotor (lids, pupils, H-pattern), facial (brow, eye closure, smile), vagus (palate, uvula, gag with IX).
UMN facial lesions spare the forehead; LMN lesions affect the whole ipsilateral face.
The course of each nerve helps localisation: compressive III palsy involves the pupil, VI palsy may be a false-localising sign, and cerebellopontine angle lesions combine VII and VIII signs.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle?

distractorRationale.a: The oculomotor nerve supplies most other extraocular muscles.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique.
distractorRationale.c: The abducens supplies the lateral rectus.
distractorRationale.d: The trigeminal nerve is sensory to the face and motor to mastication.

questions.explanation: The rule LR6 SO4 AO3 assigns the lateral rectus to CN VI, the superior oblique to CN IV and the rest to CN III.

questions.stem: Which nerve carries taste sensation from the anterior two thirds of the tongue?

options.text: Chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve
Lingual branch of the mandibular nerve alone

questions.correctOptionText: Chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve

distractorRationale.a: Correct: taste fibres of the anterior two thirds travel in the chorda tympani with the lingual nerve to the facial nerve.
distractorRationale.b: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the posterior third.
distractorRationale.c: The hypoglossal nerve is motor to the tongue.
distractorRationale.d: The lingual nerve carries general sensation, not taste, though chorda tympani joins it.

questions.explanation: Taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve. General sensation of this part is carried by the lingual nerve (V3).

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles?

distractorRationale.a: The vagus supplies pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles.
distractorRationale.b: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: CN XI supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

questions.explanation: The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Testing involves head turning against resistance and shoulder shrug.

questions.stem: On testing a 49-year-old man's eye movements, the left eye cannot adduct, elevate or depress, and rests down and out. Which accompanying findings complete the picture of a complete left oculomotor palsy?

options.text: Left ptosis and a dilated, poorly reactive pupil

questions.correctOptionText: Left ptosis and a dilated, poorly reactive pupil

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of levator palpebrae and pupillary parasympathetic fibres.
distractorRationale.b: Miosis with ptosis and enophthalmos describes Horner syndrome.
distractorRationale.d: The lateral rectus (abducens) is spared in a CN III palsy.

questions.explanation: CN III supplies the levator palpebrae and carries parasympathetic fibres to the sphincter pupillae. Its complete lesion therefore adds ptosis and a dilated pupil to the down-and-out eye.

questions.stem: A patient is asked to raise the eyebrows, close the eyes tightly and show the teeth. Which nerve is being tested?

distractorRationale.a: The trigeminal tests sensation and jaw movement.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: these movements test the muscles of facial expression.
distractorRationale.c: The hypoglossal nerve is tested by tongue protrusion.
distractorRationale.d: The accessory nerve is tested by shoulder shrug and head turn.

questions.explanation: Raising the eyebrows, tight eye closure and showing the teeth test the muscles of facial expression supplied by the facial nerve.

questions.stem: True or false: the gag reflex tests the glossopharyngeal nerve as the afferent limb and the vagus nerve as the efferent limb.
questions.explanation: Touching the posterior pharyngeal wall stimulates glossopharyngeal afferents, and the efferent response, contraction of the pharyngeal muscles, travels in the vagus nerve.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a severe headache and papilloedema has double vision on looking to the right and cannot abduct the right eye. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. What is the best explanation for the isolated right abducens palsy?

options.text: A lesion of the right oculomotor nucleus
Stretching of the long intracranial course of the abducens nerve by raised intracranial pressure
Compression of the facial nerve in the facial canal
Infarction of the right occipital lobe

questions.correctOptionText: Stretching of the long intracranial course of the abducens nerve by raised intracranial pressure

distractorRationale.a: An oculomotor lesion would cause ptosis and adduction loss.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the abducens has a long intracranial path and is a classic false-localising sign.
distractorRationale.c: Facial canal compression causes facial weakness.
distractorRationale.d: Occipital infarction causes visual field defects.

questions.explanation: Papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure. The abducens nerve's long course up the clivus and over the petrous apex makes it susceptible, and an isolated VI palsy may not indicate a lesion at its nucleus.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has a sudden painful left third nerve palsy with ptosis, a down-and-out eye and a dilated, unreactive pupil. Which cause is most important to exclude urgently?

options.text: Compression by an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery
A pituitary adenoma affecting the optic chiasm

questions.correctOptionText: Compression by an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery

distractorRationale.a: Correct: compression of the superficial pupillary fibres can produce a dilated pupil, and an aneurysm can rupture.
distractorRationale.b: Bell palsy affects the facial nerve.
distractorRationale.d: Chiasmal compression affects visual fields rather than the oculomotor nerve.

questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve runs beside the posterior communicating artery, and compression by an aneurysm typically involves the superficial parasympathetic fibres, so the pupil is dilated. This needs urgent vascular imaging because rupture can cause subarachnoid haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has progressive right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus, then numbness of the right cheek and weakness of the entire right face. Explain how a single lesion at the cerebellopontine angle can account for these signs, and state whether the facial weakness is UMN or LMN.
markingGuide: The vestibulocochlear (VIII) and facial (VII) nerves run together in the cerebellopontine angle and internal acoustic meatus
VIII involvement explains hearing loss and tinnitus
The trigeminal nerve (V) lies nearby; its involvement causes facial numbness
Facial weakness involves the whole face including the forehead, so it is LMN
The mass is likely a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
Large lesions may also compress the cerebellum or brainstem
questions.explanation: The cerebellopontine angle is the point where CN VII and VIII exit the brainstem together, with CN V close by. A mass there affects each nerve in turn, and since it damages the facial nerve itself, the weakness is lower motor neurone and involves the forehead.

questions.stem: Describe how you would test the oculomotor nerve at the bedside and what you would expect to find in a complete lesion.
markingGuide: Test direct and consensual light reflexes and accommodation
Test eye movements in an H pattern, asking about diplopia
Complete lesion: ptosis, eye down and out, dilated unreactive pupil
Lateral rectus and superior oblique unaffected
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve supplies the levator, four extraocular muscles and pupillary constrictors, so the examination covers lids, pupils and eye movements. Unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique pull the eye down and out in a complete palsy.
